title: The armor of God (Ephesians 6:10–17)
hook: truth as a belt, faith as a shield, the word as a sword

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven ones: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Your line was one lord. Which peace did you try to keep? Day five hundred eighty-six.

If you'd spent months chained to a Roman soldier, you'd know his kit by heart. The belt. The breastplate. The sandals. The big oval shield, the helmet, the short sword. Acts says that in Rome Paul lived under guard with a soldier, and in Ephesians he calls himself an ambassador in a chain. Whether or not he wrote this looking at a guard, the picture he paints at the end of the letter is unmistakable. He dresses the whole church for battle.
screen: `CHAINED TO A SOLDIER.` → `BELT, BREASTPLATE, SHIELD, SWORD.` → `A CHURCH DRESSED FOR BATTLE.`

segments.voice: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The word for the full armor is panoplia, where English gets panoply. Then Paul says who the enemy is, and it's not who you'd expect: our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the spirits of wickedness. Not people. In Paul's picture, the enemy is never the person across the table. Then he hands out the kit, piece by piece. Truth as a belt, holding everything in place. The breastplate of justice; the Douay-Rheims says justice, following the Latin, where the King James says righteousness. Feet ready with the gospel of peace. Then "the shield of faith," to quench the fiery darts of the wicked one. The helmet of salvation. And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Look at the list again. Almost everything in it is for standing, not attacking. Paul's verb is stand, over and over. The only weapon is the sword, and it's made of words: God's word. Much of this comes from the prophet Isaiah, where God himself puts on justice as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation. So the armor is God's own, lent out. Catholics have long turned this into morning prayer. An old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, attributed by tradition to Patrick, asks Christ to surround the one praying on every side, and many people pray it while getting ready for the day.
screen: `PANOPLIA: THE FULL ARMOR.` · `NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD.` · `ALMOST ALL OF IT IS FOR STANDING.` · `GOD'S OWN ARMOR, FROM ISAIAH.` · then, large: `PUT ON THE ARMOR OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dress slowly. Settle, and breathe. Starting at the top, touch your head: helmet. Your chest: breastplate. Your waist: belt. Your feet: shoes. With each one, think of one word: hope, justice, truth, peace. Then think of one thing today you'll need to stand firm against: a temptation, a lie, a fear. Not a person. If you pray, you can pray through Paul's list tomorrow morning as you get dressed. If you don't, let the four touches remind you what you want to carry into the day. The bell holds the time.
The armor of God. Paul's picture of the Christian dressed for battle: truth, justice, peace, faith, salvation and the word of God. Today's word.
Your line: put on the armor. Tomorrow morning, as you get dressed, name one piece of the armor with each piece of clothing. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray a morning offering as they begin the day, and some pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate, a prayer traditionally attributed to Patrick that asks Christ's protection on every side.

fork.setup: you're handed the armor of God. what does Paul tell you to do in it, again and again?
fork.reveal: stand: against the deceits of the devil, girt with truth, shielded by faith.

original.note: Greek: full armor (Ephesians 6:11). English 'panoply' comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a call to fight.
what it means: a call to stand firm, dressed in truth, justice, peace and faith, against evil, not people.
what a scholar hears: panoplia; the Roman soldier's kit; Isaiah 59:17, where God himself wears justice and the helmet of salvation.

sources.quoted: Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil.

notes: Acts 28:16 (Paul in Rome with a soldier guarding him) and Ephesians 6:20 ('ambassador in a chain'): the script does not claim he wrote while looking at a guard.
Check Douay-Rheims wording of 6:11 and 'the shield of faith' (6:16).
Isaiah 59:17 as background (God puts on justice as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation). Confirm.
St. Patrick's Breastplate: attributed to Patrick by tradition; many scholars date it later. Described, not quoted.
